nodes.text: The author seeks rugged offline phones over flagship ecosystems, tests Ulefone, then compares smaller brands with LLM-written scrapers.

evidence.text: For years, I've been particular about the cellphones I use. It's not just about having a phone, it's about finding one that genuinely solves my problems without forcing me into unnecessary ecosystems or gimmicks. Here's a look at how my relationship with cellphones evolved over time, from the early days of indestructible feature phones to my current obsession with rugged, no-nonsense devices.

This search led me to Ulefone, a small Chinese company specializing in rugged phones. These devices were a revelation. Ulefone phones weren't trying to compete with the likes of Apple or Samsung. Instead, they focused on solving real problems for people who needed tough, reliable devices. Here's what I loved about Ulefone: durability (waterproof, shockproof, dustproof); practical features (dual SIM, SD card slots, headphone jacks); battery life (one model lasted an entire week on a single charge); affordability (about 1/10th the price of flagship devices). I've put these phones through hell. I've dropped them countless times, taken them swimming, and generally abused them in ways that would destroy most devices. Yet they've held up remarkably well. This summer, I dived a bit too deep into a lake with my current Ulefone, and while it started acting up, it still works.

So I went searching. Recently LLM models are getting better, so I asked openAI's O1 model to give me a list of phones from smaller companies that have the features I want, 5G, e-sim, SD card, good battery, water proof, and decent camera. It gave me a bunch of them with generally wrong specs, but the model names where correct. So, I searched for them and found specs on all of them in gsmarena.com. It got hard to compare them, so again I asked gpt-4o-mini to write some python code that when I provide a list of links, scrapes the phone specs from those websites and put them in a table that I can then use to compare. Here is a modified version of the code: import requests, BeautifulSoup, pandas; def get_phone_specs(urls): session with retry strategy, session.get(url), soup = BeautifulSoup(response.content, 'html.parser'), title plus specs-list tables into phone_specs dicts; phones_df = pd.DataFrame(all_phones); return phones_df.

nodes.text: Early phones: reliable Sony Ericsson, a phoneless spell, then day-one Motorola Droid.

evidence.text: My first cellphone was a Sony Ericsson J100. It was a no-frills device, but it did what it needed to do: it was reliable, durable, and hardy. I used it without complaints, and it never let me down. For a while, I didn't even own a phone. Back then, I didn't feel the need for one. That changed with the release of the Motorola Droid, one of the first Android smartphones widely available in the U.S. I bought it on day one, and it quickly became a centerpiece of my life.

nodes.text: Smartphone disillusionment: attention traps made a consumer of him, so he retreated to dial-pad.

evidence.text: The Droid ushered in a new era for me. I explored every feature it offered and even experimented with one of the world's first smartwatches. For a while, I was captivated. My phone was a tool, an organizer, and a companion rolled into one. But the honeymoon phase didn't last. Over time, I became disillusioned with smartphones. They weren't solving problems for me; they were creating new ones. Notifications, endless customization, and attention-stealing apps made me feel more like a consumer than a user. So, I made a drastic decision: I switched to a dial-pad phone.

nodes.text: Screens, keyboards, styluses, and watches all failed the same way.

evidence.text: After a break from smartphones, I slowly ventured back into the market, testing different devices. I tried it all: small screens and large screens; physical keyboards; stylus-equipped phones; the latest smartwatches. But no matter what I tried, the result was the same: these phones were not built for people like me. They were built to sell features I didn't need, push ads I didn't want, and lock me into ecosystems I avoided. This realization shifted my focus. I started looking for phones that prioritized functionality over flashiness.

nodes.text: Requirements: battery, ruggedness, SD, jack, mic; no to cameras, AI, cloud.

evidence.text: What did I want from a phone? Long battery life; waterproofing and shockproofing; SD card slots and headphone jacks; decent mic and speaker quality; customization options. I didn't care about: having the best camera, a simple one was fine; AI enhancements in photos, frankly unnecessary; cloud storage, I preferred offline independence. The tech industry's obsession with connectivity frustrated me. Companies like Apple and Google deliberately limited options for offline use, removing SD card slots and offering minimal onboard storage to push cloud services. I wanted to take my phone to the mountains, listen to music, read, and take notes without worrying about connectivity.

nodes.text: Phones are tools, not status symbols; big brands serve profit, small ones serve needs.

evidence.text: For me, phones are tools, not status symbols. I don't want a device that decides what's important for me or forces me to conform to its limitations. I want a phone that fits into my life, solves my problems, and respects my choices. The big players in the industry, Apple, Google, Samsung, don't cater to people like me. Their focus is on creating ecosystems that prioritize profit over genuine user needs. Smaller companies like Ulefone, however, are filling that gap. If there's one thing I've learned, it's that you don't have to settle for what the market says you need. My journey with cellphones has been about rejecting trends and seeking solutions. While the world chases megapixels and AI gimmicks, I'll be here with my rugged, reliable phone, ready for whatever life throws at me.

nodes.text: A Black Friday Pixel deal triggered lock-in anxiety and collapsed on extra charges.

evidence.text: But just as black Friday was approaching I got fooled by a deal from my network provider and ordered a latest version of google pixel, people had generally good things to say about it, and I was thinking to maybe go back to the always connected life for a while to see what I was missing, but while I was waiting for the phone to arrive I was getting anxious that I knew I'm paying a hefty amount of money to first lock myself in for a couple of years and then have to pay the remaining amount to buy the phone while I knew I am not going to enjoy it because they are going to limit my choices as much as they can. Fortunately, I hadn't paid for anything yet and when the phone arrived they started to bring up some extra charges for random things which I declined and got back on the market to see what else is there to explore.

nodes.text: LLM-assisted comparison: O1 named candidates, a scraper pulled specs, Claude cleaned them.

evidence.text: So I went searching. Recently LLM models are getting better, so I asked openAI's O1 model to give me a list of phones from smaller companies that have the features I want, 5G, e-sim, SD card, good battery, water proof, and decent camera. It gave me a bunch of them with generally wrong specs, but the model names where correct. So, I searched for them and found specs on all of them in gsmarena.com. It got hard to compare them, so again I asked gpt-4o-mini to write some python code that when I provide a list of links, scrapes the phone specs from those websites and put them in a table that I can then use to compare. Here is a modified version of the code: import requests, BeautifulSoup, pandas; def get_phone_specs(urls): session with retry strategy, session.get(url), soup = BeautifulSoup(response.content, 'html.parser'), title plus specs-list tables into phone_specs dicts; phones_df = pd.DataFrame(all_phones); return phones_df.

Then I gave it the list of URLs for the phone I'm interested in: urls = [18 gsmarena links: vivo iQOO Z7, realme Narzo 60, xiaomi Poco F5 Pro, oneplus Nord N30, asus Zenfone 10, motorola Edge 40, xiaomi Redmi Note 12 Pro, nothing Phone (2), fairphone 4, realme 11 Pro+, infinix Zero Ultra, oppo A78, vivo V27e, vivo V27 Pro, tecno Phantom X2, xiaomi Poco X5 Pro, motorola Moto G Power (2024), realme Narzo 60]; df = get_phone_specs(urls); df.to_csv("smartphone_specs.csv", index=False). I wish there were websites that would allow me to do these analysis simply without scraping them.

Asking claude-3.5 sonnet for cleaning code over several prompts: def clean_phone_specs(df) extracts brand, model, has_5g, has_esim, release_year, screen_size, has_dual_sim, battery_mah, charging_speed, has_sd_slot, main_camera_mpx, selfie_camera_mpx, price_usd. I haven't checked any of this and I assume it has made several errors, but it gives a good starting point. The results are an 18-row table with columns brand | model | has_5g | has_esim | release_year | screen_size | has_dual_sim | battery_mah | charging_speed | has_sd_slot | main_camera_mpx | selfie_camera_mpx | price_usd (e.g. xiaomi Poco F5 Pro, 5160 mAh, 438.96 USD).

nodes.text: The TCL trial failed on heat and screen; the Motorola G85 is next.

evidence.text: Update 2025-01-05: I've tried the TCL 50 XE NXTPAPER for a couple of weeks. It is pretty weak in terms of performance. It got pretty hot while on a video call to the point it was uncomfortable. And worst of all, the screen wasn't at all readable in direct light, even lamp light. It definitely is less glossy, but that not only doesn't make it easier to read the screen, it makes it much much worse. The camera is so so, nothing exciting, nothing particularly bad. The paper color and ink color modes are good ideas, but not best implemented, there's lots of restrictions and not much customizable. Even going to dark mode needs tricks! I've returned it. Next I'm going to try a Motorola G85. I wanted a G75 since it is more waterproof (IP68), but I couldn't find it in any stores. G85 only has a water repellent design.
